findings.detail: `retireModel` strikes an id off on the first `isModelUnavailable(error)` hit, and nothing ever removes it from the bucket short of `resetRetiredModels()` (a test seam) or a reload. ADR-0006 makes exactly the right argument for not persisting this — "a retirement is permanent but a transient 404 is not" — but that argument applies inside a session too, and the code does not act on it there. `isModelUnavailable` matches on `not_found` / `is not found` / `404`+`model` anywhere in the message, so one transient NOT_FOUND from the API downgrades the `quality` tier to a Flash id for the rest of that key's session, silently for OCR / Compare / Web Scraper (Translate now says so via `onNotice`, which is why this is low rather than higher). The user-facing consequence is a long Translate or OCR session running on a weaker model than the user chose, with no way to recover except reloading the tab and losing the loaded workbook. What would raise this to medium is evidence that Google actually returns transient NOT_FOUND under load; absent that, the trigger is speculative and the failure direction is safe (a weaker translation, not a wrong one).
findings.summary: An in-session retirement is irreversible; only a page reload clears it

findings.detail: This PR widened `isModelUnavailable` from `any` to `unknown` (line 224) — good — but the two catch blocks it added in the same diff, `generateText` (line 556) and the restructured `processGeneralFile` loop (line 522), still annotate `catch (error: any)`. In both blocks `error` is used only as `isModelUnavailable(error)` and `throw error`, so neither needs `any`; the annotation is inherited idiom rather than a requirement. `handbooks/language/typescript/type-safety.md` flags an `: any` added in the diff without a same-line reason. This is cosmetic today, but it is the seam through which a later edit reaches for an untyped property on an error object without the compiler objecting. The pre-existing `catch (error: any)` at lines 360, 447 and 708 are outside the diff and are not flagged.
findings.summary: New catch clauses use `error: any` where `unknown` now compiles cleanly
